=== CALL C0440 ===
Gemma: Hiya. Can you hear me alright?
Kayleigh: Yeah. Yeah, I can hear you.
Gemma: Okay. Erm, I'm Gemma.
Kayleigh: Kayleigh.
Gemma: So we just sort of talk, yeah? For three minutes.
Kayleigh: Suppose so. I'm not being funny but I'm only doing it for the money, to be fair.
Gemma: Same, honestly. Student bursary doesn't exactly stretch.
Kayleigh: Student? I had you down as a nurse, from your picture. The scrubs on the airer, like.
Gemma: Yeah, nearly. Final year, so I'm on placement full time on a medical ward. Long days, nights, all of it. I did three years as a healthcare assistant before that, so I sort of know the drill.
Kayleigh: I'm a carer. Care home, older people. Twelve-hour days mostly.
Gemma: Oh, so you're in it as well. Did you just come off one? You look how I feel.
Kayleigh: Cheers.
Gemma: Sorry, that came out wrong. I just meant knackered.
Kayleigh: No, you're alright, I am knackered. Third one this week. I've still got my tunic on under this, I haven't even changed.
Gemma: Is it a decent place?
Kayleigh: Honestly? No. It's badly run, the pay's a joke, and the seniors just sit in the office doing their notes while we're running round doing everything. And then they'll have a go at you 'cause you're two minutes late for handover, when the parking's a nightmare and there's nowhere to put your car anyway. Do you know what I mean? Like, give me somewhere to park and I'll be on time.
Gemma: Yeah. When I was an HCA it was the same, the staff car park was full by seven. I don't drive in London anyway, the bus from Catford takes forever. But the seniors thing, yeah, I get that.
Kayleigh: I'd go agency tomorrow for an extra pound an hour, to be fair.
Gemma: Why don't you?
Kayleigh: Dunno really.
Gemma: Fair enough.
Kayleigh: Erm, my mum has my daughter after school, so I sort of need regular shifts. Agency's all over the place.
Gemma: How old's your daughter?
Kayleigh: Ten. Lacey. My mum does most of the pick-ups, she's ten minutes away, so that's a godsend. What about you, you got kids?
Gemma: No. Everyone keeps asking, both families. My husband wants a dog first and I keep saying no to that as well.
Kayleigh: Dogs are more work than kids, some of them.
Gemma: That's what I said. We've got a one-bed flat above a dry cleaner's, where's it going to go?
Kayleigh: Do you like it though, the nursing? 'Cause I started my Level 3 twice and never finished, it was the written bits. I couldn't be doing essays.
Gemma: The hands-on bit, yeah, I love it. Cannulas, obs, when someone's going off and you've got to be quick. The essays I hate. I've got one due Friday I haven't started, so, you know. I'm not the person to ask about writing stuff.
Kayleigh: At least you're getting a proper job out of it though. Band whatever.
Gemma: Band 5, hopefully. It's still not loads, to be honest. But better than a bursary.
Kayleigh: Anything's better than what we get. I picked up a meal deal and an energy drink on the way home and that's my tea.
Gemma: That's me on nights. Meal deal and a Twix out the vending machine at four in the morning.
Kayleigh: Living the dream, innit.
Gemma: Honestly. What did you think of that puzzle thing at the start? I didn't get the last one.
Kayleigh: I just guessed. I wasn't sitting there for ages, I've been up since half five.
Gemma: Yeah, I gave up on it as well, I was just—

=== CALL C0441 ===
Joanne: Hello? Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Gemma: Yeah. Hiya.
Joanne: Hiya. I'm Joanne. Sorry, I'm never sure if I'm doing these right. Do we just chat?
Gemma: Yeah, that's it really. I'm Gemma.
Joanne: Gemma, okay. I saw your scrubs on the airer in your photo. Are you a nurse?
Gemma: Student. Final year. On an acute medical ward at the minute.
Joanne: Oh, lovely. I'm in care, senior care assistant at a residential home near Huntingdon. Forty beds. I run the day shift, so meds rounds, handovers, the rota, all that.
Gemma: Do you like it?
Joanne: Erm... yeah. Most days. I've just done three twelves on the trot, so ask me again Thursday. I'm knackered. But I'm sort of proud of it, if I'm honest. The day shift runs properly when I'm on. It's the ones who are on their phones all shift that drive me mad.
Gemma: Yeah, we've got a couple of them. HCAs on their phones in the sluice.
Joanne: In the sluice! See, I'd have something to say about that.
Gemma: I did. Got told to soften how I say things. Again.
Joanne: No, that's rubbish, to be honest. If someone's not doing their job, you tell them. I'm the same. Some of the younger ones find me hard work, you know, but the managers don't mind.
Gemma: That's sort of what my mentor says. Good on the hands-on stuff, bad on documentation.
Joanne: Oh, documentation. I keep a paper notebook as well as the electronic records, 'cause I don't trust the system not to go down. It went down for a whole morning in March, and guess who had everything written down.
Gemma: Fair. Our e-obs freezes on nights all the time.
Joanne: There you go. What do you want to do when you qualify, then?
Gemma: Band 5 on a medical ward or A&E. Probably the same trust. Band 6 eventually. Not management.
Joanne: No, I get that. I'm doing my Level 3 leadership diploma, the home's paying for it, 'cause I want deputy manager when ours retires. But not registered manager. No way. I'm worrying weeks before a CQC inspection as it is.
Gemma: What's the diploma like? The writing bits?
Joanne: Erm, it's alright. Slow. I do it on my days off in between batch cooking. Sorry, am I going on?
Gemma: No, it's fine. I've got an essay due Friday I haven't started, so I'm not judging.
Joanne: Friday! Gemma!
Gemma: I know. I always do them the night before.
Joanne: My daughter was like that. Ellie. She's twenty, she's in Peterborough now with her boyfriend.
Gemma: Is that alright?
Joanne: ...Yeah. Sort of. She's an adult, isn't she. You can't tell them. Anyway. Is it London you're in?
Gemma: Catford. One-bed above a dry cleaner's with my husband.
Joanne: Do you get a proper dinner when you get in, or is it toast?
Gemma: Dean does most of the cooking. On nights it's a meal deal and a Twix.
Joanne: Oh, don't. I batch-cook so there's always something in the freezer, otherwise Callum, my son, would live on crisps. He's seventeen. Never puts a plate in the dishwasher, ever.
Gemma: Sounds about right.
Joanne: Do you get much time off, on placement? Do you—

=== CALL C0442 ===
Darren: Alright. Can you hear me okay?
Kayleigh: Yeah.
Darren: Sound's a bit... no, it's fine, you're there. I'm Darren.
Kayleigh: Kayleigh.
Darren: Nice one. Erm, I don't really know what we're meant to talk about. Just anything, I suppose.
Kayleigh: Dunno really.

Kayleigh: Care home. I'm a carer.
Darren: No way, so's Gemma. My partner. Residential home, older people.
Kayleigh: Funny, the girl I just had was a Gemma. Student nurse though. Where's yours work?
Darren: Just near us, Sutton-in-Ashfield. Notts. She's been doing it years. Her back's knackered from the lifting, honestly. They're meant to use the hoist with two of them, but there's never two free, so she just does it.
Kayleigh: Yeah, that's every home. I'm not being funny but they want two on a hoist and then put four of you on for thirty residents. It's a joke. And the seniors won't help, they're sat in the office.
Darren: That's what she says, word for word nearly.

Darren: Warehouse. Picking and loading at a distribution centre off the M1. Fifty-odd hours a week with the overtime. They time your breaks to the minute. Kayleigh: They're all the same, managers. They don't do the actual job.
Darren: Exactly that. Do you know what I mean, if he got on the floor for a day he'd soon change his tune.
Kayleigh: Ours wouldn't last a shift.
Darren: Is it twelve hours you do?
Kayleigh: Yeah, mostly. Forty a week. I want to stop doing them, to be fair, but you need the money.
Darren: Yeah. That's it, isn't it. Petrol, bills, everything.
Kayleigh: My car needs an MOT and I'm skint till payday. And school's asking for money for a trip again.
Darren: You got kids?
Kayleigh: Daughter. She's ten.
Darren: Nice. We haven't. Just the dog, Mabel. Staffie cross, she's about twelve now, snores like a lorry.
Kayleigh: Lacey wants a dog. Not happening.
Darren: Fair. Erm, your picture had that Live Laugh Love thing in it. Sorry, that's a weird thing to say. I just notice stuff in pictures. I draw a bit, you know. Buildings mostly.
Kayleigh: That was off my mum. I wouldn't have bought it.
Darren: Ha, no. Mine's a drawing of a pit headstock, behind me there. Bit sad, probably.
Kayleigh: No, that's alright, that. You did that?
Darren: Yeah, years ago. Did a year of art at college then packed it in.
Kayleigh: I did a year of hair and beauty and packed that in. I do nails now, on the side, like.
Darren: Yeah? Gemma'd love that, she's always—

Like, give me somewhere to park and I'll be on time.

Gemma: Why don't you?
Kayleigh: Dunno really.
Gemma: Fair enough.
Kayleigh: Erm, my mum has my daughter after school, so I sort of need regular shifts. Agency's all over the place.

Gemma: No. Everyone keeps asking, both families. My husband wants a dog first and I keep saying no to that as well.

calls.C0441:
Joanne: Hello? Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?

Joanne: Hiya. I'm Joanne. Sorry, I'm never sure if I'm doing these right. Do we just chat?
Gemma: Yeah, that's it really. I'm Gemma.
Joanne: Gemma, okay. I saw your scrubs on the airer in your photo. Are you a nurse?
Gemma: Student. Final year. On an acute medical ward at the minute.

Gemma: Do you like it?
Joanne: Erm... yeah. Most days. I've just done three twelves on the trot, so ask me again Thursday. I'm knackered. But I'm sort of proud of it, if I'm honest. The day shift runs properly when I'm on. It's the ones who are on their phones all shift that drive me mad.
Gemma: Yeah, we've got a couple of them. HCAs on their phones in the sluice.
Joanne: In the sluice! See, I'd have something to say about that.
Gemma: I did. Got told to soften how I say things. Again.
Joanne: No, that's rubbish, to be honest. If someone's not doing their job, you tell them. I'm the same. Some of the younger ones find me hard work, you know, but the managers don't mind.
Gemma: That's sort of what my mentor says. Good on the hands-on stuff, bad on documentation.
Joanne: Oh, documentation. I keep a paper notebook as well as the electronic records, 'cause I don't trust the system not to go down. It went down for a whole morning in March, and guess who had everything written down.
Gemma: Fair. Our e-obs freezes on nights all the time.
Joanne: There you go. What do you want to do when you qualify, then?
Gemma: Band 5 on a medical ward or A&E. Probably the same trust. Band 6 eventually. Not management.

Joanne: Erm, it's alright. Slow. I do it on my days off in between batch cooking. Sorry, am I going on?
Gemma: No, it's fine. I've got an essay due Friday I haven't started, so I'm not judging.

Gemma: I know. I always do them the night before.
Joanne: My daughter was like that. Ellie. She's twenty, she's in Peterborough now with her boyfriend.
Gemma: Is that alright?
Joanne: ...Yeah. Sort of. She's an adult, isn't she. You can't tell them. Anyway. Is it London you're in?
Gemma: Catford. One-bed above a dry cleaner's with my husband.
Joanne: Do you get a proper dinner when you get in, or is it toast?
Gemma: Dean does most of the cooking. On nights it's a meal deal and a Twix.
Joanne: Oh, don't. I batch-cook so there's always something in the freezer, otherwise Callum, my son, would live on crisps. He's seventeen. Never puts a plate in the dishwasher, ever.
Gemma: Sounds about right.
Joanne: Do you get much time off, on placement? Do you—
calls.C0442:

Darren: Ha, no. Mine's a drawing of a pit headstock, behind me there. Bit sad, probably.

Darren: Yeah? Gemma'd love that, she's always—
calls.C0443:

Joanne: You never. In the dress and everything?
Gareth: Full wig, mate. Kids have never let me forget it. Sorry, I'm rambling a bit there.
Joanne: No, that's made me laugh. Is there a photo? Bet there's a photo somewhere on—
